<reason>Both sides were polished and disciplined, but CON built the cleaner, surviving route to victory. A's central construct — the dilemma that a constrained sectoral table is just a statute wearing a bargaining label while an unconstrained one is an insider cartel with binding extension power — was seeded in Rebuttal 1 (A2.7), sharpened through the pressure answers, and never escaped. B's safeguards (seats, veto, limited product) all collapsed into legislation, which A accurately noted strips the motion of independent content; B's residual claim that only the table can make standards "follow the industry" was asserted rather than demonstrated and was directly answered by A's joint-liability/supply-chain statute point in the closing. B's best move — the closing concession-trap showing CON's accepted statutory floors also displace the marginal worker — genuinely dented A's exclusion weighing, but A's accountability/insider-authorship harm stood unrebutted. Both answered PQs with proper A1:/A2: labels; B's Rebuttal 1 clipping was a minor execution cost. A used plausible real-world examples (South Africa extension, Southern European dualism) without fake precision; B relied more on clean but thinner general reasoning.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.7 → A4.2: A converted B's own safeguard list into the decisive dilemma — everything that makes the table safe is legislation, so bargaining adds only insider authorship with the force of law — a burden B answered only by describing more legislation.</best_rebuttal>
